title: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Anisotropic walls and elongated cells”. Scope: elongated plant cells, algae, yeasts and other walled cells grown free of external restraint

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism gives clear directional measurements and intervention predictions. Existing plant and fungal imaging can test the principle in subsets, but direct mechanics and target-taxon coverage remain incomplete.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure directional wall extensibility and cell aspect ratio in freely growing walled cells, perturb wall anisotropy, and fit a mechanical growth model. Support requires anisotropy to precede and quantitatively predict ellipsoidal-to-cylindrical elongation, with isotropization producing rounder cells.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Turgor and cytoskeletal orientation covary with wall anisotropy.

Spirogyra-specific perturbation data are limited.

Direct wall extensibility is rarely measured with morphology.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.8
data existence: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction that an anisotropic wall yields a cylinder, and an isotropic wall a rounder cell, is a strong discriminator and has been measured in several plant and algal systems. Those paired measurements are in papers rather than a shape database, and AlgaeBase supplies only the outlines. The test is therefore available for a subset of free walled cells after compilation, not for elongated cells in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure wall anisotropy, for example cellulose microfibril orientation, against axial versus radial extension in freely grown cylindrical cells, and compare isotropic-wall mutants or treatments. Cylinders where extension is easier along the axis, and a shift toward spheres when anisotropy is lost, would support the claim; cylinders with isotropic walls, or no shape change when anisotropy is removed, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
External constraint is hard to rule out for cells inside a filament.

Microfibril angle and growth anisotropy are published for model cells, not archived with the algal images.

Turgor pressure is a necessary partner of wall anisotropy, so the wall is not the sole variable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.5
